entry.title: Basic concepts of <blockquote>
entry.content:
title: Basic concepts of <blockquote>
slug: Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/Blockquote/Basic_concepts
page-type: guide
sidebar: htmlsidebar

The <blockquote> HTML element represents a section of content that is a quotation from another source. It is generally displayed as an indented block and is used for longer quotations.

This article explains the main features of <blockquote> and shows how to use it effectively.

Content and structure

A <blockquote> can contain any block-level content, including paragraphs, lists, and other elements. The source of the quotation is usually cited using <p> and <cite>.

Example:

<div>
  <blockquote cite="https://www.huxley.net/bnw/four.html">
    <p>
      Words can be like X-rays, if you use them properly—they’ll go through
      anything. You read and you’re pierced.
    </p>
  </blockquote>
  <p>—Aldous Huxley, <cite>Brave New World</cite></p>
</div>

{{EmbedLiveSample("blockquote-basic")}}

cite attribute

The cite attribute provides the URL or reference of the source. It does not affect the visual rendering, but is useful for semantics and accessibility.

Example:

<div>
  <blockquote cite="https://example.com/famous-quote">
    <p>"Practice makes perfect."</p>
  </blockquote>
  <p>—Example Author, <cite>Example Work</cite></p>
</div>

{{EmbedLiveSample("blockquote-cite")}}

Best practices

  • Use <blockquote> only for quotations from other sources.
  • Combine <blockquote> with <p> for authorship and <cite> for the work’s title.
  • Avoid using <blockquote> purely for visual indentation; use CSS for styling instead.
  • For short inline quotations, prefer <q> instead of <blockquote>.

Summary:

  • <blockquote>: long quotations.
  • <q>: short inline quotations.
  • cite: URL of the source.
  • <p>: paragraph of quote or author.
  • <div>: container block.
  • <cite>: title of the work.

Basic and Logical Concepts of

1. Multiple paragraphs

<blockquote cite="https://www.huxley.net/bnw/four.html" style="padding:10px; border-left:3px solid #006caf; background-color:#f0f8ff;">
  <p>Words can be like X-rays, if you use them properly—they’ll go through anything.</p>
  <p>You read and you’re pierced.</p>
</blockquote>
<p>—Aldous Huxley, <cite>Brave New World</cite></p>

2. Nested blockquotes

<blockquote cite="https://www.huxley.net/bnw/four.html" style="padding:10px; border-left:3px solid #006caf; background-color:#e6f2ff;">
  <p>"Words can be like X-rays..."</p>
  <blockquote cite="https://www.huxley.net/bnw/intro.html" style="margin-left:2em; border-left:2px solid #0099ff; padding:5px;">
    <p>"This is a nested quotation."</p>
  </blockquote>
</blockquote>

3. Using <cite>

<blockquote style="padding:10px; border-left:3px solid #006caf; background-color:#f9f9f9;">
  <p>"Knowledge is power."</p>
  <footer>—Francis Bacon, <cite>The Advancement of Learning</cite></footer>
</blockquote>

4. Headings inside blockquotes

<blockquote cite="https://example.com/article" style="padding:10px; border-left:3px solid #006caf; background-color:#e0f7ff;">
  <h3>Important note:</h3>
  <p>This is a quotation with a heading.</p>
</blockquote>

5. Lists inside blockquotes

<blockquote cite="https://example.com" style="padding:10px; border-left:3px solid #006caf; background-color:#f0f0ff;">
  <p>Key points:</p>
  <ul>
    <li>First point</li>
    <li>Second point</li>
    <li>Third point</li>
  </ul>
</blockquote>

6. Nested formatting

<blockquote cite="https://example.com/article" style="padding:10px; border-left:3px solid #006caf; background-color:#fff0f0;">
  <p>
    <strong>Important:</strong> Always check your sources. <em>Accuracy matters</em>. 
    See more at <a href="https://example.com">Example</a>.
  </p>
</blockquote>

7. Using <footer>

<blockquote cite="https://www.huxley.net/bnw/four.html" style="padding:10px; border-left:3px solid #006caf; background-color:#f0fff0;">
  <p>"Words can be like X-rays, if you use them properly—they’ll go through anything."</p>
  <footer>—Aldous Huxley, <cite>Brave New World</cite></footer>
</blockquote>

Logical and Basic Concepts of <blockquote>

Semantic Meaning

Blockquotes are semantically used to quote another source.
Always include the cite attribute when referencing the source.

<blockquote cite="https://www.huxley.net/bnw/four.html">
  <p>Words can be like X-rays, if you use them properly—they’ll go through anything.</p>
</blockquote>
<p>—Aldous Huxley, <cite>Brave New World</cite></p>

Start and End Edges

Blockquotes respect the writing direction (LTR or RTL).
The start edge aligns with the start of the text flow, and the end edge aligns with the end.

<blockquote style="margin-inline-start:2em; border-left:3px solid #006caf; padding:10px;">
  <p>This quotation respects the start and end edges according to writing mode.</p>
</blockquote>

Accessibility

Blockquotes should be accessible:

  • Use <p> for paragraphs inside
  • Use <cite> for the source
  • Avoid putting interactive content inside unless necessary
<blockquote cite="https://www.huxley.net/bnw/four.html">
  <p>Accessible blockquotes improve screen reader support.</p>
  <footer>—Aldous Huxley, <cite>Brave New World</cite></footer>
</blockquote>

Nesting and Hierarchy

Blockquotes can be nested to show hierarchy or quoting layers.

<blockquote>
  <p>Outer quote.</p>
  <blockquote>
    <p>Nested quote inside the outer quote.</p>
  </blockquote>
</blockquote>

Visual Distinction

Although logical, adding visual cues like borders or background colors improves readability.

<blockquote style="padding:10px; border-left:3px solid #006caf; background-color:#f0f8ff;">
  <p>Visual distinction helps separate quoted content from main content.</p>
</blockquote>

Diagrams

The diagram below is a example of using one blockquote in wikidot

-//-
The diagram below is a brown blockquote, it can make blockquote width and height impact

-//-

Programming Concepts

Tag / Attribute Concept / Purpose Example
<blockquote> Semantically marks a section as a quotation from another source. <blockquote cite="https://example.com">Quoted text here.</blockquote>
cite Specifies the URL of the source of the quotation. <blockquote cite="https://www.huxley.net/bnw/four.html">...</blockquote>
<p> Paragraphs inside a blockquote; keeps content structured. <blockquote><p>Quote text.</p></blockquote>
<footer> Optional element for attribution or citation. <blockquote><p>Quote</p><footer>—Author, <cite>Source</cite></footer></blockquote>
<cite> References the source title of the quotation. <footer>—Author, <cite>Title</cite></footer>
Nested <blockquote> Allows hierarchy of quotations. <blockquote>Outer<p><blockquote>Inner quote</blockquote></p></blockquote>
style Can define visual distinction (borders, padding, background). <blockquote style="border-left:3px solid #006caf;">Quote</blockquote>
-//-

Tools and Concepts for <blockquote>

Blockquotes can be enhanced using various tools and techniques to improve readability, styling, and semantic structure.

1. Browser and Editor Tools

Most code editors and browsers can render blockquotes directly.

  • Editors like VS Code, Sublime Text, or GitHub’s Markdown preview render blockquotes with proper indentation.
  • Browser DevTools let you inspect <blockquote> elements, their styles, and computed properties.
<blockquote cite="https://www.huxley.net/bnw/four.html">
  <p>Words can be like X-rays, if you use them properly—they’ll go through anything.</p>
</blockquote>

2. Styling Tools

CSS properties help visually distinguish blockquotes:

  • border-left or border-start
  • background-color
  • padding and margin
  • Typography: font-style: italic; or font-family
<blockquote style="border-left:4px solid #006caf; padding:10px; background-color:#f0f8ff; font-style:italic;">
  <p>This blockquote uses CSS styling tools for emphasis.</p>
</blockquote>

3. Semantic Tools

Proper use of semantic elements ensures accessibility:

  • <cite> for sources
  • <footer> for attribution
  • <p> for structured paragraphs
  • Nested <blockquote> for layered quotes
<blockquote cite="https://www.huxley.net/bnw/four.html">
  <p>Nested quotes are supported.</p>
  <blockquote>
    <p>This is a nested quotation.</p>
  </blockquote>
  <footer>—Aldous Huxley, <cite>Brave New World</cite></footer>
</blockquote>

4. Interactive Tools

Blockquotes can be combined with interactive elements in a safe, semantic way:

  • Buttons for “Read More” inside the container (not inside the <p> itself)
  • Anchors <a> for source linking
  • Tooltips for context
<blockquote style="border-left:3px solid #006caf; padding:10px; background-color:#e6f7ff;">
  <p>Click the link below for full context:</p>
  <a href="https://www.huxley.net/bnw/four.html" target="_blank">Read the full source</a>
</blockquote>

5. Combining Tools

You can mix styling, semantic structure, and interactivity to create accessible, readable, and visually distinct blockquotes.

<blockquote cite="https://www.huxley.net/bnw/four.html" style="border-left:4px solid #006caf; padding:12px; background-color:#f0f8ff;">
  <h3>Quote of the Day</h3>
  <p>Words can be like X-rays, if you use them properly—they’ll go through anything.</p>
  <footer>—Aldous Huxley, <cite>Brave New World</cite></footer>
  <a href="https://www.huxley.net/bnw/four.html" target="_blank">Source</a>
</blockquote>

Compatibility Concepts of <blockquote>

Blockquotes are widely supported, but understanding compatibility ensures correct rendering across browsers, devices, and Markdown platforms.

1. Browser Support

  • <blockquote> is fully supported in all modern browsers (Chrome, Firefox, Safari, Edge, Opera).
  • CSS styling properties like border-left, padding, and background-color are also widely supported.
<blockquote style="border-left:3px solid #006caf; padding:10px; background-color:#f0f8ff;">
  <p>This blockquote will render consistently across modern browsers.</p>
</blockquote>

2. Markdown Support

  • Most Markdown parsers (GitHub, GitLab, Markdown-it) support blockquotes using the > character.
  • HTML <blockquote> can also be used directly in Markdown for custom styling.
> This is a blockquote in Markdown
> 
> Supports multiple paragraphs and lists.
<blockquote>
  <p>This is the same quote but using HTML inside Markdown for custom styling.</p>
</blockquote>

3. Nested Blockquote Compatibility

  • Nested blockquotes work consistently in HTML and Markdown, though Markdown requires >> or additional > for nesting.
  • CSS margin-left or padding-left can help visually distinguish nested quotes.
<blockquote style="border-left:3px solid #006caf; padding:10px;">
  <p>Outer blockquote.</p>
  <blockquote style="border-left:2px solid #0099ff; padding:5px;">
    <p>Nested blockquote inside.</p>
  </blockquote>
</blockquote>

4. Responsive Compatibility

  • Blockquotes should be responsive, especially when using CSS styling:
    • Avoid fixed widths
    • Use relative units (em, %)
    • Ensure text wraps properly on smaller screens
<blockquote style="border-left:3px solid #006caf; padding:1em; background-color:#f0f8ff; max-width:90%;">
  <p>This blockquote adapts to screen size using relative units and max-width.</p>
</blockquote>

5. Accessibility Considerations

  • Use semantic HTML (<p>, <cite>, <footer>) to improve screen reader support.
  • Avoid interactive elements inside paragraphs unless necessary.
<blockquote cite="https://www.huxley.net/bnw/four.html">
  <p>Accessible blockquotes are compatible with screen readers and assistive technologies.</p>
  <footer>—Aldous Huxley, <cite>Brave New World</cite></footer>
</blockquote>

Practical Guide to Using <blockquote> Concepts

This guide shows how to apply basic, logical, and compatible blockquote concepts in your HTML and Markdown projects.

1. Using a Basic Blockquote

Start with a simple quote wrapped in <blockquote> with a <p> for the text and <cite> for the source.

<blockquote cite="https://www.huxley.net/bnw/four.html" style="border-left:3px solid #006caf; padding:10px; background-color:#f0f8ff;">
  <p>Words can be like X-rays, if you use them properly—they’ll go through anything.</p>
</blockquote>
<p>—Aldous Huxley, <cite>Brave New World</cite></p>

2. Adding Semantic Structure

Include <footer> for attribution and <cite> for the source to improve semantic meaning and accessibility.

<blockquote cite="https://www.huxley.net/bnw/four.html">
  <p>This quote uses semantic elements for proper attribution.</p>
  <footer>—Aldous Huxley, <cite>Brave New World</cite></footer>
</blockquote>

3. Nested Blockquotes

Use nested <blockquote> elements for quoting within a quote.
Add visual cues like borders or margin to indicate hierarchy.

<blockquote style="border-left:3px solid #006caf; padding:10px;">
  <p>Outer blockquote</p>
  <blockquote style="border-left:2px solid #0099ff; padding:5px;">
    <p>Nested blockquote inside</p>
  </blockquote>
</blockquote>

4. Styling Blockquotes

Use CSS to create visual distinction: borders, background-color, padding, font style, etc.

<blockquote style="border-left:4px solid #006caf; padding:12px; background-color:#f0f8ff; font-style:italic;">
  <p>This blockquote is visually styled for emphasis.</p>
</blockquote>

5. Responsive and Accessible Blockquotes

Ensure blockquotes adapt to different screen sizes and are readable by assistive technologies.

<blockquote style="border-left:3px solid #006caf; padding:1em; max-width:90%; background-color:#f0f8ff;">
  <p>Responsive and accessible blockquote example.</p>
  <footer>—Author Name, <cite>Source</cite></footer>
</blockquote>

6. Combining Concepts

You can combine all concepts: semantic structure, nested quotes, styling, accessibility, and responsiveness.

<blockquote cite="https://www.huxley.net/bnw/four.html" style="border-left:4px solid #006caf; padding:12px; background-color:#e6f7ff;">
  <h3>Quote of the Day</h3>
  <p>Words can be like X-rays, if you use them properly—they’ll go through anything.</p>
  <blockquote style="border-left:2px solid #0099ff; padding:5px; margin-top:5px;">
    <p>Nested emphasis: nested quotes can highlight subtext or commentary.</p>
  </blockquote>
  <footer>—Aldous Huxley, <cite>Brave New World</cite></footer>
  <a href="https://www.huxley.net/bnw/four.html" target="_blank">Source</a>
</blockquote>

entry.content:
This PR improves the documentation by explaining how invoker commands and the button command attribute interact with dialogs, and adds a small example demonstrating their usage.

entry.title: TrustedTypes: SVGAnimatedString.baseVal
entry.content:
The SVGAnimatedString can represent the base and animated values of various elements in SVG.

In the context of SVGScriptElement.href it can be used to set the baseVal of the script. This is an injection sink.

Technically right place for all the information is SVGAnimatedString.baseVal since that defines the property, but that can be used to reflect numerous attributes, and only one is a problem case. So what I have done is put TT info in the SVGScriptElement.href. For SVGAnimatedString.baseVal I have put the disclaimer and explanation, but I link to the other doc for security considerations and the example.

Related docs work tracked in #41507

entry.title: fix: mention that pre doesn't strip leading '\n' in XML
entry.content:
That is a feature of the HTML syntax parsing rules, not the HTML abstract language itself, hence does not apply when using the XML syntax of HTML (also known as XHTML).

The HTML standard notes this as:

In the HTML syntax, a leading newline character immediately following the pre element start tag is stripped.

entry.title: TrustedTypes: Function() constructor + eval()
entry.content:
The Function() constructor can execute its arguments as JavaScript.
Similarly eval() executes its input as JavaScript.

This updates the TrustedType information for both methods.

Note, I provided an example for eval() but not Function. I wasn't sure if I should do either, because even though this is notionally safer than not using trusted types, there is really no direction on how you can practically and generically transform a script so that it is safe.

For the eval() case I just indicated the use of custom transforming function, for which I provided no implementation. For Function, I added a disclaimer and linked to the eval() example.

Related docs work tracked in #41507

entry.title: Fix `display` toggle in playground not changing value
entry.content:
Description

Changes a <select> value in a playground to be read after each change of the <select>, correctly reacting to the change.

Motivation

The display: flow-root playground has a <select> toggle, which is supposed to change the display value of some elements to demonstrate the effects of the flow-root value.

Currently, its value is read only once when the playground JS is first executed, which results in display: block always getting set on the elements.
